projects.title: Mosaics of Urban Giardino
descriptions: In Sicily, the term giardino has always meant productive orchard before it translates directly to garden. Amidst Siracusa's climate crisis and petrochemical legacy, its fertile giardini that once wove centuries of cultivation have been displaced, leaving a biome fractured.

The Orchard Living Lab proposes to restore harmony between human settlement and productive nature. Reinterpreting traditional Sicilian agriculture and Mediterranean food practices, the scheme returns the giardino Mediterraneo to the heart of the urban block, with the citrus tree at its centre as the structural anchor, seasonal clock and ecological engine of the whole.

The scheme aims to become a living biome animated by cycles of growth, exchange and regeneration, in which every element feeds the next. Its inhabitants, human and non-human alike, are active stewards in sustaining a landscape that sustains them in return, through the reciprocal relationship between people, place and production.

images.caption: Giardino Mediterraneo - a single citrus tree protected by a circular dry stone wall: a device as much as climatic and spatial.
Coltura promiscua - interplanting fruit trees with vines, cereals, legumes and understorey herbs.

Citrus came to Sicily with the Arabs in the 9th century. The Siracusa lemon accounts for a third of Italy's total lemon output, which is prized for its yield and quality. The simultaneity of flower and fruit on the same branch made it a symbol of the orchard at its most abundant.
A single citrus tree planted at the centre of the Living Lab recreates the Giardino Mediterraneo, integrated with stone amphitheatre seating, performs as the social anchor of the scheme

Developing from the giardino Mediterraneo, planting spaces are organized as a series of interlocking “negative” mosaics, carved from the mass of the site and aligned along the primary axis, opening to the south to receive sunlight.
Spatial strategy and programme traces growth, exchange, inhabitation and regeneration; massing strategy.
The existing carpark of Piazza Adda is transformed into a market, shops and the dining hall opens up to the vibrant street frontage.
Existing condition of Piazza Adda
Proposed condition of Piazza Adda, the ground floor is shaded by a colonnade while perforated shutters provides a sound and visual barrier to enhance user privacy in the storeys above.
Lower Ground Floor Plan
Upper Ground Floor Plan
First Floor Plan

While residential use begins from the first floor, the activities of growing, exchanging and regenerating the orchard mainly dictates the upper ground floor and lower ground floor. At each stage, flora is taken into a new form and the building traces its life cycle.
Main gateway to the building, the orangerie is visually connected to the pavement.
The orangerie, a winter garden testing what Siracusa might grow next, such as tropical species introduced as the climate warms

Set within an urban fabric defined by concrete residential buildings, the Orchard Living Lab reframes material selection through the lens of locality, ecological impact and what its surrounding already contain. The process begins with identifying what the land contains, including its remnants, its excesses and its latent resources, acknowledging that can be reused, cultivated and transformed rather than imported.

The long section traces a continuous journey from arrival to inhabitation, cutting through the entrance foyer, the orangerie and into the productive agroforestry grounds before descending into the giardino mediterraneo.
The understorey approaching the giardino Mediterraneo (Rhino, Enscape, Photoshop)

Each level offers different growing conditions, shaded hollows for moisture-dependent plants and suspended planting strung from overhead wires between walkways. The elevated walkways threads through the layers.

Inspired by the logic of coltura promiscua, an independent exoskeleton structure sits outside the thermal envelope, as a living, breathing edge that extends domestic space, shelters non-human residents and performs as a growing facade.
Vertical louvres and tensioned wire guides provide a climbing structure for plants across the facade, simultaneously giving solar shading for spaces behind it.
The southeast coast of Siracusa is a major arrival point for bird migrating north from Africa. Bird boxes for Sicilian Hoopoe are integrated within the roof.
1:20 detail model of bird nooks integrated within the roof of the cooking patio, which is supported by rammed earth.
Vertical louvres simultaneously become both shading devices and trellises for climbing plants. Terracotta swift bricks are integrated into the planter base
From the first floor, the building's programme is mainly residential.
The Dining Hall
The dining hall blurs the boundary between private dwelling and public realm, with its north facade opening towards the market.
Above, residential balconies form a colonnade that invites public movement. The units share a continuous balcony, create a semi-private threshold for dwelling and making.
The drying tower makes the drying process visible, operates as a passive climate device without mechanical assistance or insulation
The Drying Tower
The Recyclab, a waste resource facility that transforms pruning waste from the orchard and organic waste from the community kitchen into useful resources such as heat, energy and new materials.
The recyclab's orchard interface continues the rammed earth language expressed throughout.

projects.title: Syraka
descriptions: The Masterplan proposes a regenerative vision for Siracusa through integrating environmental resilience, social infrastructure and strategic phasing. Drawing on the city's etymological roots in Syraka, meaning a city with an abundance of water, the masterplan responds to contemporary challenges of drought and pollution from its petrochemical legacy.

As the city transitions towards clean energy, climate-resilient agriculture and sustainable tourism, water is repositioned as the driver of regeneration, transforming it from a scarce resource into an urban, ecological and social catalyst. This vision is articulated through the Loop, an intersecting blue-green system where land meets water.

The Loop forms a continuous infrastructure for infiltration, attenuation and retention through reactivating historic quarries, river channels and the coastline. The strategy supports regional mobility, climate adaptation and heritage revival, while guiding controlled densification to limit sprawl, envisioning a regenerative model for Siracusa and Sicily.

To diversify the city's water supply to eliminate drought vulnerability, one of the key strategies is rainwater capture and retention. Reviving abandoned quarries plays a role in adapting to seasonal rainfall, they capture rain, runoff and infiltration during the wet months.

Beyond water management, each of the eight quarries are dedicated to a specific agricultural use, fostering research, education, and community participation. Around this agricultural framework, we have designed community zones for art and culture, civic gathering, and recreation—returning the quarries to the people.
The three quarries in the arts and culture zone are designed in detail and are connected by a botanical garden
The proposed theatre reactivates Latomia della intagliatell, offering a contemporary counterpart to the Greek and Roman theatres of the Neapolis archaeological park.
Urban tool kit inspired by the indigenous agricultural technique coltura promiscua.
The forgotten ruins will be improved by removing overgrowth, providing information and allowing closer public access via boardwalks.
Easy-assembly market stalls built from the urban tool kit of timber parts
Piazza Adda Carpark transformed into a vibrant food market, surrounding residential buildings retrofitted with an exoskeleton timber structure
Using the ‘Coltura Promiscua’ Kit of Parts to enhance the new city park, supporting a range of activities around the Lido, including sports and allotments.
The lido provides a large public space for people to interact with water whilst also coming together and socialising.
Using the ‘Coltura Promiscua’ Kit of parts to create floating boardwalks so that people can observe the sea grass intervention which aims to feed marine life and sequester carbon

The seagrass nursery strengthens Siracusa’s wider blue belt by enhancing marine biodiversity and improving water quality, acting as a natural carbon sink. This further links ecological resilience and cultivation practices within the city’s broader vision of sustainable marine stewardship.

projects.title: MycoCycle Studio
descriptions: Informed by finger-shaped peninsulas designed in a group masterplan on Saxonvale, the rectilinear mycelium brick workshop is a place for production, discovery and community. Combining traditional agricultural heritage with contemporary innovation in materiality, the project aims to position Frome as a pioneer in circular economy, where buildings grow, decompose, and return to the earth.

Drawn from the subterranean imagery of mycelium weaving through soil and the woodland atmosphere of where mushrooms grow, the workshop is structured like a tree: 

Roots — an energy-giving component, where mushrooms grow. 

Trunk — services and circulation, pumping mycelium nurtures from underground to the fabrication workshop. 

Canopy — exposed structure capturing light and rain.
Visitors trace this vertical journey through tree-like structures, experiencing the mushroom's life cycle and symbolically becoming part of the forest network.

Isometric render of the lower ground floor shows the meandering path of the visitor journey. The movements mirrors the interconnected layout of rooms on ground floor, both reflecting the complex network of mycelium weaving through the soil.

The undercroft space features the discvoery roots and sculptural furniture. The flooring combines stone paving and gravel, while a rendered ceiling with LEDs creates a cave-like atmosphere that remains softly illuminated.

Isometric render of the upper ground floor and first floor, the spiraling movement of the tree walk is designed to echo the way mushrooms emerge from the ground, resonating with the narrative that connects visitors’ spatial experience to the lifecycle of fungi.

projects.title: Lucy's Room
projects.type: Music Therapy Centre for Warneford Hospital
descriptions: Lucy Sessions, a young mother living with emotionally unstable disorder, found her only comfort in practicing music. After her passing in 2017, her parents partnered with Oxford Health Charity to propose a music room at Warneford Hospital, Oxford. Their initiative highlighted the potential of music as a therapeutic tool for mental health. This project, inspired by Lucy's story, celebrates the healing power of music through spaces designed for sensory experiences, restoration, education and community engagement.

Awarded the Prize for Environmental Design & Wellbeing, the proposal adopts a protective courtyard form, surrounding the garden are music rooms resembling potted plants to symbolise nurture and growth. The palette of materials, lighting, acoustics and landscapes, underpinned by biophilic principles and sustainable systems, supports therapy and music use. Comfort and sustainability guide the design, positively shaping user experience and the building's life cycle.

projects.title: South West Campus
descriptions: I was heavily involved in the creative process, from concept generation at tender stage to finalizing the design and preparing all architectural drawings for planning. In response to PolyU's long-standing need for flexible, high capacity academic and research space, the south west redevelopment of A Wing and GH Annex delivers a 15 storey building with 19,400 sqm of usable space, providing laboratories, workshops, classrooms, study areas, communal facilities, and offices.

The design enhances the university's identity by extending the campus' podium for improved connectivity. The lower levels introduce stepping terraces with planting to reduce impact at street level and retaining PolyU's signature red brick. Above, curved glass facades and metal cladding of the 'tower' contrast with its solid base, symbolising the balanced values of heritage and innovation at the university.

projects.title: Waterway Bridge
projects.type: Dongguan Taiping Waterway Bridge Design Competition
descriptions: As a placement student, I was responsible for digital modeling, diagramming and a full set of architectural drawings for the competition submission. The proposal was awarded the Gold Winner for its world-class pedestrian-motorway bridge design.

The tied-arch bridge features a 370m main span with a steel box girder deck supported by hanger cables and compression arches. The concept integrated green space planning, water transport, city lighting and carbon reduction strategies. The design integrates the district's masterplan, celebrating the city and water, day and night, natural and man-made landscapes.

The bridge creates a sustainable, multi-modal crossing that separates motorized and slow traffic, with pedestrian platforms hovering over the motorway that offer views of the bay, enhancing connectivity and public experience.

about.name: Joyce Lee
about.title: Part II Architectural Assistant
about.bio:
Part II architectural assistant and MArch candidate at the University of Bath (graduating summer 2026), with 2.5 years of practice experience across Wilkinson Eyre, LWK + Partners and CaSA Architects.

I work across the full design arc — concept research, iterative development, 3D modelling, rendering and presentation — with a focus on turning complex information into clear, review-ready drawings and narratives. I collaborate easily across multidisciplinary teams, pick up new tools fast, and deliver to tight deadlines.

items.desc: Contributed to a range of building types including waterfront development, elderly homes, children's care centres, universities and hospitals across RIBA Stages 0-4, coordinating with clients and consultants. Polytechnic University South West Campus (RIBA Stages 0-3): produced drawings, diagrams, renders and presentations. Po Leung Kuk Service for the Elderly (RIBA Stages 3-4): led detailed design and statutory submissions, including the team's first full technical package in Revit. BIM Coordination: developed a Revit package to streamline technical design and GBP submissions; hosted an in-house seminar on BIM workflows.
Worked across RIBA Stages 1-3 on residential projects of varying scales, including home extensions and refurbishment of existing house fabric and form.

Dongguan Taiping Waterway Bridge: assisted in creating digital models, diagrams and drawings for the competition submission. University of Hong Kong Business School: part of the interiors team for RIBA Stage 3; involved in digital modelling, rendering, video editing, report presentation and coordinating with material suppliers.
